A preposition is a word that shows the relationship between two things in a sentence — usually between a noun (or pronoun) and some other part of the sentence.

Think of it this way: things in the real world are always related to each other in some way — one thing is near another, one event happens before another, one action is done for someone. A preposition is the word that captures and expresses that relationship.
A Simple Example First

The cat sat on the mat.

Here, on is the preposition. It tells you the relationship between the cat and the mat — specifically, a relationship of position (the cat is positioned on top of the mat). Without on, you'd just have "The cat sat the mat," which makes no sense.
What Kinds of Relationships Do Prepositions Express?

Prepositions are incredibly versatile. They can express many different types of relationships:

Place / Position

The keys are on the table. The dog is under the bed. She lives in London. He stood beside me.

Direction / Movement

He walked into the room. She ran towards the door. The plane flew over the city. They went through the tunnel.

Time

I'll see you at noon. She arrived before me. We met during the summer. He slept until morning.

Cause or Reason

He was late because of the traffic. She cried from exhaustion.

Purpose

This knife is for cutting vegetables. She studied hard for the exam.

Means or Method

He came by train. She paid with cash. Write it in pencil.

Association or Belonging

A cup of tea. The president of the country. A friend of mine.

Against or Concerning

She argued against the plan. We talked about the problem.

These categories are not rigid — the same preposition can express different types of relationships depending on context, and the list above is not exhaustive.
The Prepositional Phrase

A preposition almost never travels alone. It works with a noun (or pronoun) that follows it. This combination — preposition + noun/pronoun — is called a prepositional phrase.

in the morning → the whole phrase tells you when
under the bridge → tells you where
for her birthday → tells you the purpose/occasion
with him → tells you who accompanied the action

The noun or pronoun that comes after the preposition is called the object of the preposition. The preposition sets up the relationship; its object is one of the two things being related.

She is sitting next to [preposition] the window [object].
Where Prepositions Sit in a Sentence

The word "preposition" contains "pre" (meaning before) and "position" — because a preposition is typically placed before its object. This is its usual position in English.

He ran through the forest. ✅ (through comes before the forest)

However, in everyday English — especially in speech and informal writing — it is perfectly natural and accepted to place a preposition at the end of a sentence, particularly in questions and relative clauses:

What are you talking about?
This is the house I grew up in.
Who are you waiting for?

There is an old-fashioned rule that says you should never end a sentence with a preposition, but this rule is largely considered outdated and overly rigid today. Most grammarians and writers agree that ending a sentence with a preposition is fine, and that forcing a sentence to avoid it often makes it sound stiff and unnatural.
Common Prepositions

Here are some of the most frequently used prepositions in English:

Simple prepositions (single words):
about, above, across, after, against, along, among, around, at, before, behind, below, beneath, beside, between, beyond, by, down, during, except, for, from, in, inside, into, like, near, of, off, on, onto, out, outside, over, past, since, through, throughout, till, to, toward, under, until, up, upon, with, within, without

Compound prepositions (made of more than one word — also called "complex prepositions"):
according to, ahead of, as well as, because of, close to, due to, except for, in addition to, in front of, in spite of, instead of, next to, on behalf of, on top of, out of, thanks to, together with, up to
How to Identify a Preposition

A reliable test: ask if the word expresses a relationship between a noun/pronoun and something else, and check whether you can slot it into the classic test phrase — "the [blank] the box" — using place-related prepositions:

in the box, on the box, under the box, behind the box, beside the box, through the box…

If the word fits into this kind of frame and connects two elements meaningfully, it's likely a preposition. Of course, prepositions that deal with time, cause, or purpose don't fit the box test, but the principle — that it links a noun/pronoun to something else in the sentence — remains the same.
An Important Nuance: Same Word, Different Job

Many words that act as prepositions can also serve as other parts of speech depending on how they're used. This can be confusing at first.

For example, before can be a preposition or a conjunction:

She left before sunset. → preposition (before + noun sunset)
She left before the sun set. → conjunction (links two clauses)

Similarly, up can be a preposition, an adverb, or even a verb:

He walked up the stairs. → preposition
He looked up. → adverb (no object follows it)

The key rule: a preposition must have an object (a noun or pronoun after it). If the word stands alone without an object, it's functioning as something else — usually an adverb.
Why Prepositions Matter

Without prepositions, language would be incredibly clumsy. Compare:

She put the book. She went the library. He is the chair.

vs.

She put the book on the shelf. She went to the library. He is sitting in the chair.

Prepositions quietly do enormous work — they glue ideas together, clarify meaning, and show how actions, objects, people, and events relate to one another in space, time, and logic. They are small words, but they carry enormous precision.
Summary

A preposition is a word (or group of words) that expresses a relationship — of place, time, direction, cause, purpose, manner, or association — between a noun or pronoun and another part of the sentence. It comes before its object to form a prepositional phrase, and that phrase functions as a unit to give additional information about where, when, why, how, or with/against/for whom something happens.
